name: Japanese
genre_traditions: J-pop is the dominant modern form but sits alongside genuinely distinct traditions: enka (演歌), whose kobushi vibrato and openly sentimental register read as retro and formal rather than sincere to younger listeners; city pop, urbane and often melancholy under a bright surface; anime tie-up songs, written to carry a story's emotional argument in four minutes; Vocaloid/net music, where dense, fast, syllable-packed writing is the idiom; and folk (min'yō) and shōwa-era kayōkyoku. Behind all of them sits the classical poetic tradition — waka, haiku, tanka — which counts morae rather than rhyming and prizes implication over statement. Identify which the song is working in: enka's directness and city pop's cool detachment are opposite emotional strategies and must not be flattened into 'ballad'.
register_axis: Three axes operate at once, and Japanese is unusual in how much they carry. First, politeness level: plain form (だ/である) versus polite (です/ます) versus keigo proper — lyrics almost always use plain form, so any shift into polite speech is a deliberate act of distance or formality. Second, the first-person pronoun, which is characterization rather than grammar: 僕 (boku, soft/young/often male), 俺 (ore, blunt, assertive), 私 (watashi, neutral or formal), あたし (atashi, casual feminine), わたくし (formal). Choosing one sets who is speaking before a single image appears. Third — and easy to miss — the SCRIPT itself is register: the same word written in kanji, hiragana, or katakana feels different. Hiragana softens and slows; katakana can read as cold, foreign, mechanical, or emphatic; kanji is denser and more formal. A lyricist writing あなた rather than 貴方, or putting a native word in katakana, is making a tonal choice English has no direct equivalent for.
rhyme_convention: Traditional Japanese verse does not rhyme. Its formal structure is MORA COUNT — haiku 5-7-5, tanka 5-7-5-7-7 — and Japanese phonology makes rhyme nearly automatic and therefore uninformative (most words end in one of five vowels). What carries structure instead: mora counts against the melody, repetition, parallelism, and assonance. Rhyme in J-pop and Japanese hip-hop is a consciously borrowed English device and should read as borrowed rather than native when it appears. Do not treat the absence of rhyme as formlessness — the form is somewhere else.
symbol_calibration: Archetypal WITHIN Japanese lyric and poetry, and therefore NOT to be flagged as exotic or culturally specific: cherry blossom (桜) for beauty that matters because it ends; cicadas (蝉) for the pressure and transience of summer; snow for stilled time; fireworks (花火) for a brief shared brightness; the sea for distance and scale; rain for grief or waiting; the moon; and seasonal reference generally — the classical kigo tradition means naming a season IS naming an emotional register, not scene-setting. Also unmarked: train stations and platforms for parting, the school classroom and its window for adolescence, and convenience-store/streetlight imagery in modern city pop. An English reader will hear several of these as distinctively Japanese; within the tradition they are commonplaces, and marking them as culturally specific mis-routes the Cultural Historian.
structural_traps: Subjects are omitted constantly — far more than in Hindi, Korean or Spanish — and a Japanese lyric can run for lines with no stated subject at all. English forces you to supply one, and supplying the WRONG one silently invents a narrative. Say in leans_into when you inferred who is acting, and consider whether the source's refusal to specify is itself the effect.

The first-person pronoun (僕/俺/私/あたし) characterizes the speaker's gender, age, and self-presentation. English 'I' erases all of it. Note which was used — it is often the clearest evidence of who is singing.

Sentence-final particles (ね、よ、な、かな、わ、ぞ) carry emotional stance: seeking agreement, asserting, musing, softening. They are not translatable as words and vanish silently in English. Their loss flattens a line's attitude; note where the source used them.
Japanese does not mark plural, and often does not mark tense the way English requires. Do not invent a number or a tense the source leaves open — sometimes the openness is the point.
Name suffixes (-さん, -ちゃん, -くん, -先輩) encode relationship and distance with no English equivalent. Dropping them loses the relationship; keeping them raw can read as untranslated.
は versus が determines what is foregrounded as topic rather than merely stated. English word order and stress must carry that, and getting it backwards inverts a line's emphasis.

Script choice is tonal (see register_axis). If a lyricist writes a word in hiragana where kanji is normal, or in katakana for a native word, something is being said about tone that plain English cannot mirror — flag it rather than ignoring it.
grammatical_scaffolding_note: Japanese is SOV, marks grammatical roles with particles (は/が/を/に/で) rather than word order, drops subjects and objects freely, and puts modifiers before what they modify. Reordering into English SVO, supplying the omitted subject/object, and adding the articles and plural marking English requires are all scaffolding needed to parse and do NOT count against the Compression Floor. What does count: adding 'because', 'even though', 'so that', or 'which' to explain a relation the source left to juxtaposition — Japanese lyric writing leans heavily on bare juxtaposition of images, and English's instinct to connect them with logic is precisely the failure this law exists to catch.
emotional_baseline: This is the most important calibration for Japanese, and the one an English-trained model gets wrong by default. Japanese lyric convention reaches strong feeling INDIRECTLY — through an image, a season, a physical detail, or a thing left unsaid — and stating the emotion outright is marked, not neutral. The classical sensibility here is もののあはれ (mono no aware): feeling that arises from noticing something passing, held rather than declared. A model's instinct is to render 'the cherry blossoms fall' as something about grief and loss; that is not translation, it is explanation, and it destroys the exact effect the line was built for. If the source reaches its feeling through an image, reaching it through the image IS the faithful rendering. Restraint is the default and understatement is the norm — but note the exceptions: enka, and the climactic chorus of many J-pop ballads, ARE direct, and imposing uniform restraint on a song that deliberately breaks into open statement is its own mistranslation. Match the source's strategy, not a stereotype of Japanese restraint.

anchor_lexicon.meaning: a chest-tightening ache that mixes love, sadness and longing without being simply any of them — extremely common in lyrics and with no single English word
the warm gladness of something remembered — nostalgia without English nostalgia's sadness

anchor_lexicon.term: もののあはれ (mono no aware)
anchor_lexicon.meaning: the gentle sadness of things passing; the classical sensibility underlying much Japanese lyric restraint
beauty found in imperfection, incompleteness and age
sunlight filtering through leaves — a single word for a thing English needs a clause for
a profound, mysterious depth that is suggested rather than shown
the wish to depend on and be indulged by someone close, presumed rather than requested
